words.definition: Free from restrictions or controls; able to act without limits.
words.example: Once the strict curfew was lifted, the students enjoyed an unfettered summer of late-night adventures.
words.mnemonic: un- (not) + fetter (a foot chain): picture the chains cut off your ankles so you can run free.

words.definition: Able to govern oneself and act independently without outside control.
words.example: The region operates as an autonomous zone, setting its own laws without approval from the central government.
words.mnemonic: auto (self) + nomos (law) = 'self-law', like an auto that drives itself with no one at the wheel.

words.definition: Having supreme authority and full independent control over a territory.
words.example: The small island became a sovereign nation, answering to no foreign power after the treaty was signed.
words.mnemonic: Break it into 'so-reign': the one who reigns above all — picture a lone crowned monarch on a throne.

words.definition: To keep someone or something within set boundaries or a small space.
words.example: The vet told us to confine the recovering puppy to one quiet room until its leg healed.
words.mnemonic: con- + 'fine': imagine being fined and boxed into a tiny cell as your punishment.

words.definition: A chain or metal band placed on the feet to prevent movement.
words.example: The prisoner shuffled slowly across the yard, each step limited by the heavy fetter around his ankles.
words.mnemonic: It rhymes with 'better', but a chain on your 'feet' makes nothing better — feet + iron.

words.definition: A metal ring or cuff used to bind a person's wrists or ankles.
words.example: The museum displayed a rusted shackle once clamped onto the wrists of enslaved workers.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'shake + cackle': a captive shakes the iron cuffs while the jailer cackles.

words.definition: A rope or chain that ties something to a fixed spot.
words.example: The goat could graze only in a small circle, kept close by the tether staked to the ground.
words.mnemonic: Rhymes with 'feather': picture a light balloon tied on a string so it can't float away.

words.definition: The condition of being enslaved or held under another person's total control.
words.example: The novel follows a family's escape from generations of bondage on a cotton plantation.
words.mnemonic: 'bond' + age: ties (bonds) that hold you for an age — ropes you cannot loosen.

words.definition: The state of being confined and unable to leave or escape freely.
words.example: The rescued eagle had spent so long in captivity that it had forgotten how to hunt.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'captive city': a walled city you are held inside and cannot leave.

words.definition: To lock someone up and hold them against their will.
words.example: The corrupt regime would imprison anyone who dared to criticize its leader in public.
words.mnemonic: Literally 'im- (in) + prison': to put someone IN a PRISON.

words.definition: To confine a person in a jail or penal institution.
words.example: Judges may incarcerate repeat offenders for years, even for relatively minor crimes.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'carcer' (prison): to put someone into the 'carcer' — in-CARCER-ate.

words.definition: To hold someone officially, preventing them from leaving.
words.example: Airport security may detain a traveler for questioning if their documents seem suspicious.
words.mnemonic: de- + 'tain' (Latin tenere, to hold): think 'delay + retain' — you are held back from leaving.

words.definition: Threats or force used to make someone act against their will.
words.example: She later argued the contract was invalid because she had signed it under duress.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'do-or-stress': from Latin 'durus' (hard) — hard pressure forcing you to act.

words.definition: To make someone the property of another and force their labor.
words.example: Colonizers would enslave entire populations to work the sugar and coffee fields.
words.mnemonic: en- (to make) + 'slave': to turn a free person into a slave — chains and forced work.

words.definition: The condition of being forced to work for another without freedom.
words.example: The workers were trapped in a form of servitude, laboring for years just to pay off a fake debt.
words.mnemonic: 'serve' + -itude: a lasting state of forced serving — a servant with no way out.

words.definition: Rescue or release from danger, bondage, or serious difficulty.
words.example: After forty days lost at sea, the sight of a rescue ship felt like deliverance.
words.mnemonic: de-LIVER-ance — picture a hero who 'delivers' you out of danger.

words.definition: Not held back or controlled in any way.
words.example: The crowd greeted the last-minute winning goal with unbridled joy.
words.mnemonic: A horse with no bridle runs wild — nothing on its head to rein it in.

words.definition: To hold back, slow down, or discourage an action or process.
words.example: Cold weather can inhibit the growth of these tropical plants.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'in-habit' — a habit that keeps you in and holds you back.

words.definition: To force someone or something into silence or block free expression.
words.example: The new law tried to muzzle journalists who criticized the government.
words.mnemonic: A dog's muzzle straps over its mouth so it can't bark or bite.

words.definition: To examine material and remove parts judged unacceptable or harmful.
words.example: The studio cut several scenes to censor the film before its teen release.
words.mnemonic: A censor grabs 'scissors' (censors) to snip out the objectionable bits.

words.definition: An official order that stops trade or exchange with a country.
words.example: The oil embargo left drivers waiting in long lines at empty gas stations.
words.mnemonic: em-BAR-go — a 'bar' slammed down so goods can't go.

words.definition: A period of isolation used to stop the spread of disease.
words.example: The sick travelers were kept in quarantine for two weeks before release.
words.mnemonic: From Italian 'quaranta' (forty) — plague ships waited forty days offshore.

words.definition: To shut away in a quiet, secluded place, apart from the world.
words.example: The scholar cloistered himself in the library for months to finish his book.
words.mnemonic: A cloister is a monastery where monks live 'closed' off — cloister/closed.

words.definition: To keep apart or hidden from other people.
words.example: They secluded themselves in a remote cabin far from any neighbors.
words.mnemonic: se- (apart) + clude (close) — closed off, away from everyone.

words.definition: To catch or trick someone into a situation they cannot escape.
words.example: The spider's sticky web entrapped every insect that flew too close.
words.mnemonic: en- + trap — literally to put someone 'in a trap.'

words.definition: Freedom to act, think, or choose within wide limits.
words.example: Her boss gave her plenty of latitude to design the project as she saw fit.
words.mnemonic: Latitude lines wrap the whole globe — lots of room, lots of freedom.

words.definition: Extra room or flexibility to move, act, or make decisions.
words.example: Leaving early gave us enough leeway to reach the airport despite the traffic.
words.mnemonic: On a boat the sheltered 'lee' side gives room to drift safely — a margin.

words.definition: A special right or privilege belonging to a particular person or group.
words.example: Naming the newborn was the mother's prerogative alone.
words.mnemonic: pre- (before) + rogative (ask) — a king was asked first; it was his exclusive right.

words.definition: Free from limits, rules, or forces that hold something back.
words.example: In the empty field the puppy ran unconstrained, chasing every falling leaf.
words.mnemonic: un- + constrained — the opposite of tied down; no straps on it at all.

words.definition: Not limited or hampered by anything; completely free.
words.example: The artist enjoyed untrammeled freedom to paint whatever she imagined.
words.mnemonic: A 'trammel' is a net or shackle — un-trammeled means no net can hold you.

words.definition: A system where a single ruler holds unlimited power over everyone else.
words.example: Under the general's autocracy, no law could pass without his personal signature.
words.mnemonic: auto- (self) + -cracy (rule): one person rules entirely by self, answering to no one.

words.definition: Supreme control or authority over a territory or people.
words.example: The empire held dominion over lands stretching from the sea to the mountains.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'dominate' — the domain you dominate becomes your dominion.

words.definition: The condition of being under another's power, like a slave.
words.example: Held in thrall by the sorcerer, the villagers obeyed his every command.
words.mnemonic: Thrall lives inside 'enthrall' — captivated and captive, held completely.

words.definition: A binding contract forcing a person to work for another for a set time.
words.example: He signed an indenture that bound him to the shipyard for seven years.
words.mnemonic: In-DENT-ure: the old contract had a 'dented' notched edge — and it bit into your freedom.

words.definition: To organize people or things into a strict, controlled system.
words.example: The headmaster tried to regiment every minute of the students' day.
words.mnemonic: A military regiment marches in rigid rows — to regiment is to force that order onto life.

words.definition: To control or have power over someone or something completely.
words.example: One loud voice can dominate a meeting so that no one else gets to speak.
words.mnemonic: Picture a 'dome' — you stand on top of it, above and over everyone below.

words.definition: To force someone to leave a place, usually as a punishment.
words.example: The king chose to banish the traitor rather than execute him.
words.mnemonic: Ban + vanish: you're banned, so now vanish — be gone from here.

words.definition: To officially force someone to leave a school, group, or place.
words.example: The school will expel any student caught cheating on the final exam.
words.mnemonic: ex- (out) + -pel (push, as in 'propel'): literally pushed out.

words.definition: To move someone or something to a lower or less important rank.
words.example: After a losing season, the team was relegated to the second division.
words.mnemonic: RE-LEG-ate: sent back to the last 'leg' of the race — down to the bottom.

words.definition: To keep someone or something separate and alone, apart from others.
words.example: Doctors isolate patients with contagious diseases to protect everyone else.
words.mnemonic: 'Isola' is Italian for island — to isolate is to make an island of someone.

words.definition: The sealing off of a place to stop goods or people from entering or leaving.
words.example: The navy set up a blockade so no ships could reach the enemy port.
words.mnemonic: Block + -ade: a barricade that blocks the way both in and out.

words.definition: To break a rule or law, or to intrude on someone's rights.
words.example: Copying that logo would infringe on the company's trademark.
words.mnemonic: Hear 'in-fringe' — stepping onto the fringe, the edge of someone else's territory.

words.definition: To take power, a position, or rights by force and without the right to.
words.example: The general plotted to usurp the throne while the queen was away.
words.mnemonic: 'You slurp' up power that isn't yours — usurp: slurping up someone else's authority.

words.definition: Choosing a strict, simple life that avoids comfort and pleasure.
words.example: The monk led an ascetic life, sleeping on a bare floor and eating only rice.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'acidic' — a bitter, austere life with none of the sweetness.

words.definition: Very deep in meaning, feeling, or knowledge.
words.example: Her speech had a profound effect on everyone who heard it.
words.mnemonic: pro- + -found (Latin 'fundus', bottom): reaching all the way to the bottom — very deep.

words.definition: Calmness and steadiness of mind, especially under stress or difficulty.
words.example: Even as the plane hit turbulence, she sipped her tea with perfect equanimity.
words.mnemonic: Equal + animus (mind): keeping an 'equal mind' no matter what happens.

words.definition: Full of noise, confusion, or violent disorder.
words.example: The crowd gave a tumultuous welcome, stamping and roaring as the champion stepped out.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'too-much-tuous' — too much commotion happening all at once.

words.definition: A harsh, jarring mixture of sounds heard together.
words.example: A cacophony of car horns, drills, and shouting rose from the street below.
words.mnemonic: Greek kakos (bad) + phone (sound) = literally 'bad sound.'

words.definition: A lack of harmony or agreement between sounds, ideas, or feelings.
words.example: There was a clear dissonance between his cheerful words and his trembling hands.
words.mnemonic: dis- (apart) + -sonance (sound): sounds or ideas that pull apart.

words.definition: Expressing feelings or opinions loudly and forcefully.
words.example: The fans were vociferous in their protest, chanting until the referee reversed the call.
words.mnemonic: voci- (voice, like 'vocal') + -ferous (carrying): carrying a very loud voice.

words.definition: To put limits on what someone can do or how much of something exists.
words.example: The new rules restrict visitors to two hours inside the gallery.
words.mnemonic: Re-STRICT: being strict again, tightening the rules around you.

words.definition: To suddenly release a powerful force or feeling that was held back.
words.example: One careless comment was enough to unleash years of pent-up anger.
words.mnemonic: un- + leash: take the leash off the dog and let it run wild.

words.definition: The state of being free to act, speak, or think as one wishes.
words.example: After years in prison, he savored the simple liberty of walking wherever he pleased.
words.mnemonic: Latin liber = free; the same root as 'liberate' and 'liberal.'

words.definition: A ruler who holds absolute power and uses it cruelly.
words.example: Under the despot, a single critical word could cost a family their home.
words.mnemonic: From Greek despotes, 'master' — picture a ruler who puts you 'on the spot' and crushes you.

words.definition: Willing to obey others completely and put their wishes first.
words.example: He was so subservient to his boss that he never once voiced his own opinion.
words.mnemonic: sub- (under) + serve: serving from underneath, below everyone else.

words.definition: Relating to a government that controls every part of people's lives.
words.example: In the totalitarian state, even private letters were read by government censors.
words.mnemonic: Built on 'total' — the regime demands total control over everything.

words.definition: A laborer in feudal times bound to work a master's land.
words.example: As a serf, he could not leave the estate or marry without the lord's permission.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'serve' — he serves the lord and the land, stuck in place.

words.definition: A wooden crossbar joining animals, or a figurative burden of oppression.
words.example: The colonies finally threw off the yoke of the empire and declared themselves free.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'yolk,' but a yoke is a heavy bar pressing down on an ox's neck.

words.definition: To make narrower or tighter, limiting movement or flow.
words.example: The tight collar seemed to constrict his throat until he could barely swallow.
words.mnemonic: con- (together) + strict: drawn tightly together, like a boa constrictor squeezing.

words.definition: Using power in a cruel, unfair, and controlling way.
words.example: The tyrannical manager fired anyone who dared to question his decisions.
words.mnemonic: From 'tyrant' — a tyrannical boss rules like a cruel tyrant of old.

words.definition: A person in charge of running a prison or supervising a specific place or rule.
words.example: The warden walked the cell block each morning, jangling the keys that locked every gate behind him.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like "guard-en" — a warden GUARDs the pen (prison).

words.definition: A metal band or chain fastened around the wrists to restrain a person.
words.example: The guard snapped a cold iron manacle onto each of the captive's wrists before the march.
words.mnemonic: "MAN + shackle" — a shackle clamped on a man's hands.

words.definition: The act of forcing someone to do something through threats or pressure.
words.example: She signed the contract only under coercion, after they threatened to fire her husband.
words.mnemonic: "CO-erce" shares its root with "force" — think of being FORCED together against your will.
